en: Rough and harsh; causing irritation in manner
hook: ABRASIVE: like sandpaper SCRAPING.
story: Abrasive. Rough and harsh in manner; irritating. Ruben's new manager at a downtown bank was brilliant with numbers but abrasive with people. He corrected staff loudly in front of customers, groaned at every question, and never said thank you. Within a month, two clerks had asked for transfers, and Ruben went home each evening feeling scraped raw. Abrasive comes from abrade, to scrape away; sandpaper is an abrasive. An abrasive person rubs everyone the wrong way. So, what word describes a manner so harsh it rubs people raw? ... Abrasive.

gre.s: Though his insights were often brilliant, the critic's ____ manner alienated many colleagues, who found his relentless sarcasm exhausting.
gre.clue: who found his relentless sarcasm exhausting

example: The new captain's abrasive style unsettled the squad, and by midseason several senior players had stopped speaking to him.

en: To quiet someone's anger, often by granting what they want
bn: তুষ্ট করা; দাবি মেনে শান্ত করা
hook: APPEASE: give them 'A PEACE' offering so they stop fighting.
story: Appease. To calm someone's anger, often by giving them what they want. Six-year-old Molly was furious. Her cousins had eaten the last piece of her birthday cake, and she sat on the stairs with her arms crossed, refusing to speak. Her grandmother came out holding a bowl of rice pudding and the promise of a new kite. Slowly, Molly [chuckle] uncrossed her arms. The pudding appeased her. Appease comes from an old French phrase meaning to bring to peace: you appease someone when you restore their peace. So, what verb means to calm someone's anger by giving them what they want? ... Appease.

gre.s: Hoping to ____ the striking workers, management offered a modest raise, though it refused their central demand for shorter hours.
gre.clue: management offered a modest raise

example: To appease fans furious about the cancelled concert, the organisers promised full refunds and a free show the following spring.

en: Confident and forceful in stating one's views or rights
hook: ASSERTIVE: firmly ASSERTS what she wants.
story: Assertive. Confident and firm in stating your views or rights. At her first team meeting, Rachel noticed a senior colleague presenting her idea as his own. Her heart pounded. In the past she would have stayed silent. This time she said, calmly and clearly, "That was my proposal. I'd like to explain the rest of it." The room went quiet, then the director nodded. Rachel had been assertive, not rude. To be assertive is to assert your view, standing firm without shouting. So, what word describes someone who states their rights firmly and confidently? ... Assertive.

gre.s: Once timid in meetings, the young analyst became increasingly ____, confidently defending her proposals against senior colleagues.
gre.clue: confidently defending her proposals against senior colleagues

example: A short course in negotiation helped Farzana become more assertive when asking clients to settle their overdue invoices.

en: To increase the size or amount of something
hook: AUGMENT: like AUGMENTED reality adding layers to the world.
story: Augment. To increase the size or amount of something. Kurt earned a modest salary as a small-town schoolteacher. To pay for his daughter's university fees, he began giving evening maths lessons on his veranda, and on weekends he sold honey from his brother's hives. Slowly, these small earnings augmented his income. When his daughter's admission letter came, he [laugh] read it aloud to the whole lane. Augment comes from the Latin for increase, the same root as auction, where the price keeps rising. So, what verb means to make something bigger? ... Augment.

gre.s: Because her scholarship barely covered tuition, she took a part-time job to ____ her income, adding enough each month to pay the rent.
gre.clue: adding enough each month to pay the rent

example: The museum augmented its small collection of Mughal miniatures with a generous loan from a private collector.

en: A picture or description that exaggerates features for comic effect
hook: CARICATURE: a CARtoon that exaggerates.
story: Caricature. A picture or description that exaggerates features for comic effect. At the city book fair, Sonya sat on a plastic stool while a young artist sketched her. Two minutes later he turned the paper around: huge eyes, a tiny chin, and glasses as big as bicycle wheels. Sonya [laugh] covered her mouth. It was a perfect caricature, unmistakably her. Caricature comes from an Italian word meaning to load: a caricature is overloaded with exaggeration. So, what word names a drawing that exaggerates someone's features for fun? ... Caricature.

gre.s: The novel's portrait of the professor is less a realistic character study than a ____: his vanity is so inflated and his absent-mindedness so extreme that no reader could mistake him for a real person.
gre.clue: no reader could mistake him for a real person

example: The film reduces the scientist to a caricature, a wild-haired genius who mutters equations and forgets to eat.

en: Done in secret, usually because it is not allowed
hook: CLANDESTINE: a secret CLAN meeting in the DESTINY hour of midnight.
story: Clandestine. Done in secret, usually because it is not allowed. In Ricky's university dorm, cooking was strictly forbidden. Yet every Thursday night, after the warden's lights went out, Ricky and three friends met in a back room with a tiny electric cooker and a packet of noodles. They whispered, kept a towel under the door, and [chuckle] froze at every footstep. Those clandestine dinners became the best memory of their first year. Hear clan inside clandestine: picture a small secret clan meeting behind a closed door. So, what word describes something done secretly because it is not allowed? ... Clandestine.

gre.s: The two rival companies held ____ talks for months, keeping the negotiations hidden even from their own boards of directors.
gre.clue: keeping the negotiations hidden even from their own boards

example: Customs officers uncovered a clandestine workshop in Chattogram where fake medicines were packed into genuine-looking boxes.

en: Self-satisfied and unaware of possible dangers or shortcomings
hook: COMPLACENT: so COMfortable in their PLACE that they stop trying.
story: Complacent. Self-satisfied and unaware of possible dangers. After scoring well on his first GRE practice test, Tim stopped studying. "I already know enough," he told his friends, and spent the next six weeks watching cricket. On test day, the reading passages were harder than anything he had seen. He walked out [sigh] knowing he had been complacent. Complacent comes from the Latin for very pleased, the same root as please: a complacent person is too pleased with himself to see danger coming. So, what word describes someone so self-satisfied that he stops trying? ... Complacent.

gre.s: Having won the championship three years in a row, the team grew ____, skipping practices and underestimating opponents they once feared.
gre.clue: skipping practices and underestimating opponents

example: Years without a serious flood had made the town's officials complacent, and the drains had not been cleaned in a decade.

en: Making a certain outcome likely; helpful
hook: CONDUCIVE: CONDUCTS you toward a result.
story: Conducive. Making a certain outcome likely; helpful. Lisa's family flat was loud: a television, three cousins, and a pressure cooker whistling every hour. Her grades kept slipping. Then her aunt offered a quiet back room with a window facing a mango tree. With silence, good light and a cup of tea at nine, Lisa studied better than ever. The room was conducive to study. Conducive is related to conduct, to lead: a conducive setting leads you toward a result. Do not confuse it with conclusive. So, what word describes conditions that help something happen? ... Conducive.

gre.s: Critics argued that the open-plan office, with its constant chatter and interruptions, was hardly ____ to the deep concentration that serious research demands.
gre.clue: with its constant chatter and interruptions

example: Warm, humid air is highly conducive to the growth of mould, so archivists keep old manuscripts in cool, dry rooms.

en: To have a mutual relationship in which one thing affects or depends on another
hook: CO-RELATE: RELATED together.
story: Correlate. To be connected so that when one thing changes, the other tends to change too. For a school project, Scott recorded how many hours his classmates slept and their maths scores. As he plotted the dots, a pattern appeared: students who slept more tended to score higher. The two clearly correlated. His teacher smiled and added a warning: correlation does not prove that one causes the other. Correlate is simply co plus relate: two things related together. So, what verb means that two things rise and fall together? ... Correlate.

gre.s: Although rates of the two diseases tend to ____, researchers have found no evidence that one actually causes the other.
gre.clue: researchers have found no evidence that one actually causes the other

example: In the survey, the number of trees on a street correlated closely with how safe residents felt walking there at night.

en: Clever at achieving goals through deceit
hook: CRAFTY: CRAFTS clever tricks.
story: Crafty. Clever at getting what you want through tricks or deceit. Every afternoon at the big city market, one fish seller sprinkled water on his tired fish so they gleamed as if fresh from the river. Customers crowded around. Nina's mother leaned close, pressed one gently with her finger, and smelled it. Then she smiled and walked on to the next stall. The seller was crafty, but she was craftier. Craft first meant skill, so a crafty person uses skill to fool others. So, what word describes someone cleverly deceitful? ... Crafty.

gre.s: The ____ negotiator concealed his true objectives behind a show of friendly candor, leading his rivals to concede far more than they had ever intended.
gre.clue: concealed his true objectives behind a show of friendly candor

example: In the old folktale, a crafty jackal persuades the crocodile gripping his leg that it has only caught a tree root.

en: Contemptibly cowardly
hook: CRAVEN: the opposite of a brave RAVEN, it flies away at any danger.
story: Craven. Shamefully cowardly. On a crowded city bus, a man began harassing a college student. Brad, a big, strong passenger, saw everything, then looked out of the window and pretended to sleep. It was an elderly woman who stood up and shouted until the man got off. Later, Brad felt ashamed of his craven silence. Craven rhymes with raven: picture a big black raven that flaps away at the first sign of trouble, leaving others to face it. So, what word means contemptibly cowardly? ... Craven.

gre.s: Historians have judged the general's retreat as ____, since he abandoned his troops at the first sign of danger.
gre.clue: abandoned his troops at the first sign of danger

example: The board's craven silence, while the founder bullied junior staff for years, shocked investors when the truth finally came out.

en: So harmful that it leaves someone weak or unable to function
hook: DE-BILITATE: removes your ABILITY.
story: Debilitating. So harmful that it leaves someone weak or unable to function. When chikungunya struck Faith in her final year, the fever lasted only a few days, but the joint pain that followed was debilitating. For a month she could not climb the stairs to her classroom without stopping to rest. Her friends brought notes, and her mother cooked soft rice and lentils every day. Slowly her strength returned. Hear ability inside debilitating: a debilitating illness takes your ability away. So, what word describes something that leaves you too weak to function? ... Debilitating.

gre.s: For years she suffered from ____ migraines, which sometimes confined her to a dark room for days at a time.
gre.clue: confined her to a dark room for days at a time

example: A debilitating shortage of trained nurses forced the rural hospital to close two of its four wards.

en: To publicly declare something wrong or evil
hook: DE-NOUNCE: ANNOUNCE it's bad.
story: Denounce. To publicly declare something wrong or evil. When a factory upstream began pouring dye into the river near Sean's village, the water turned purple and the fish died. Sean, a young schoolteacher, stood up at a public meeting and denounced the factory in front of journalists and local officials. His voice shook, but he did not stop. Within a month the dumping was investigated. Denounce shares a root with announce: to denounce something is to announce loudly that it is wrong. So, what verb means to condemn something publicly? ... Denounce.

gre.s: Human rights groups were quick to ____ the arrests, calling them a blatant attempt to silence the government's most outspoken critics.
gre.clue: calling them a blatant attempt to silence the government's most outspoken critics

example: The football federation denounced the racist chanting from the stands and fined the home club heavily.

en: To take apart; to gradually end a system
hook: DIS-MANTLE: remove the MANTLE (covering) piece by piece.
story: Dismantle. To take something apart piece by piece; also, to gradually end a system. After the spring fair ended, Megan watched the workers dismantle the giant bamboo stage. First the cloth banners came down, then the lights, then each pole, untied and stacked on a truck. By evening, the field was empty grass again. Laws and systems can be dismantled the same way, one piece at a time. A mantle is a cloak; to dismantle was first to strip off the cloak, then to take everything apart. So, what verb means to take something apart piece by piece? ... Dismantle.

gre.s: The new administration promised not merely to reform the corrupt licensing system but to ____ it entirely, replacing the old agency with an independent commission.
gre.clue: not merely to reform the corrupt licensing system

example: After the festival, volunteers dismantled the bamboo stage in a single night and stacked the poles neatly for next year.

en: Fluent, persuasive, and expressive in speaking or writing
hook: E-LOQU-ENT: 'loqu' means speak. Speaks beautifully.
story: Eloquent. Fluent, persuasive and expressive in speaking or writing. At an inter-university debate, Jules was the last speaker. The hall was noisy and tired. Then he began, softly, with a story about his mother selling vegetables to pay his fees. His words were simple, clear and full of feeling. By the end, the hall was silent, and some judges were wiping their eyes. He had been truly eloquent. Eloquent comes from the Latin loqui, to speak: an eloquent person speaks out beautifully. So, what word describes a speaker who is fluent and moving? ... Eloquent.

gre.s: Though the senator was famously awkward in live debates, his written speeches were remarkably ____, moving even his opponents with their clarity and grace.
gre.clue: moving even his opponents with their clarity and grace

example: Her eloquent letter to the city council, describing the children who played beside an open drain, won funding for a covered sewer.

en: No longer close or friendly with someone; separated
hook: ESTRANGED: became STRANGERS.
story: Estranged. No longer close or friendly; separated. Rosa and her elder brother had not spoken for eight years after a quarrel over their father's land. They lived in the same city but never visited. Then, at a cousin's wedding, they found themselves at the same table. Her brother pushed a plate of sweets toward her and quietly asked about her children. The estranged siblings talked until midnight. Estranged contains strange: estranged people have become strangers to each other. So, what word describes family members who are no longer close? ... Estranged.

gre.s: After decades of silence, the ____ siblings were finally reconciled at their mother's bedside.
gre.clue: After decades of silence

example: The novel follows an estranged father and daughter who are forced to share a car on a long drive across Spain.

en: Lacking physical strength; weak and unconvincing
hook: FEEBLE: sounds weak, like a FEEBLE 'meh'.
story: Feeble. Lacking strength; also, weak and unconvincing. Hailey's grandfather was once the strongest boatman on the river. Now, at ninety, his grip is feeble, and he needs her arm to cross the courtyard, though his voice is still steady when he tells stories of river storms. That same week, Hailey's little brother offered a feeble excuse for missing school: [chuckle] the goat had eaten his homework. Feeble sounds like a weak little bleat, the cry of a tired lamb. So, what word describes something weak, whether a grip or an excuse? ... Feeble.

gre.s: The company's ____ response to the crisis, a single vague press release issued a week late, only deepened customers' anger.
gre.clue: a single vague press release issued a week late

example: Rakib's feeble excuse that a goat had eaten his homework only made the teacher laugh.

en: Not serious; silly or unimportant
hook: FRIVOLOUS: FREE-and-VOLUME-less, no weight, no seriousness.
story: Frivolous. Not serious; silly or unimportant. Two weeks before his final exams, Alex spent an entire evening choosing a new ringtone, then another hour arranging his apps by colour. His roommate, buried in past papers, looked up and said, "Your exams are in fourteen days." Alex knew it. His evening had been completely frivolous. In court, too, a frivolous complaint is one too silly to deserve serious time. Frivolous sounds a little like frills: pretty decoration with no real purpose. So, what word describes something silly and not worth serious attention? ... Frivolous.

gre.s: The judge dismissed the lawsuit as ____, noting that the plaintiff had suffered no harm whatsoever.
gre.clue: had suffered no harm whatsoever

example: The committee wasted an hour on frivolous questions about napkin colours while the real budget problem went undiscussed.

en: Made of parts that are all alike; the same throughout
hook: HOMO = same, GENE = kind. Same kind all through.
story: Homogeneous. Made of parts that are all alike; the same throughout. Tammy's grandmother taught her to make bread dough. "Knead until it is the same everywhere," she said. "No dry spots, no lumps." Tammy kneaded until her arms ached, then pressed it: smooth, soft, perfectly homogeneous. A homogeneous group is one where every member is alike. Homo means same and genos means kind, so homogeneous means of the same kind throughout. Its opposite is heterogeneous, mixed. So, what word describes a mixture that is the same all the way through? ... Homogeneous.

gre.s: Once thought to be culturally ____, the region turns out to have been a patchwork of distinct languages and customs.
gre.clue: turns out to have been a patchwork

example: Geologists drilled cores at several points to check whether the rock layer was homogeneous or held pockets of other minerals.

en: Causing harm slowly and quietly, so it is hard to notice
hook: INSIDIOUS: sneaks INSIDE you quietly.
story: Insidious. Causing harm slowly and quietly, so it is hard to notice. For years, the tube well in Robin's village gave clear, cool water. Nobody suspected anything. But it carried arsenic, and slowly, over a decade, dark spots appeared on the hands of the old men who drank from it most. A health worker finally tested the water and painted the well red. The danger had been insidious. Insidious comes from the Latin for ambush: an insidious threat lies quietly in wait. So, what word describes harm that creeps in slowly and unnoticed? ... Insidious.

gre.s: The danger of the pollutant lies in its ____ nature: it accumulates in the body slowly and without symptoms, causing irreversible harm long before it can be detected.
gre.clue: slowly and without symptoms

example: Office gossip can have an insidious effect on a team, slowly eroding trust until colleagues stop sharing ideas.

en: Twisted together; closely connected
hook: INTER-TWINED: TWINE twisted together.
story: Intertwined. Twisted together; closely connected. Every morning, Olive passes an old banyan tree outside her school, where a vine has climbed the trunk and wound around every branch. Nobody can tell anymore where the tree ends and the vine begins. Olive thinks of her two grandmothers, best friends since childhood, whose lives are just as intertwined: same village, same school, and now the same grandchildren. To twine is to twist, and inter means between: intertwined things are twisted around each other. So, what word describes two things closely twisted together? ... Intertwined.

gre.s: In the novelist's vision, the fates of the two families are so ____ that no misfortune can befall one without eventually striking the other.
gre.clue: no misfortune can befall one without eventually striking the other

example: Behind the television, the cables had become so intertwined that tracing a single wire took Kamal half an hour.

en: Anger
hook: IRE: IRATE = angry.
story: Ire. Anger. Sam parked his motorbike across a narrow lane in the old city and ran into a sweet shop for five minutes. When he came back, a rickshaw, two vans and a furious fish seller were waiting. The fish seller's ire was magnificent: red face, waving arms, and a speech the whole lane could hear. Sam [sigh] apologised and moved the bike at once. Ire is the root of irate, which means very angry; both come from the Latin ira, anger. So, what short word means anger? ... Ire.

gre.s: The new tax on mobile data drew the ____ of students across the country, who staged noisy protests outside the ministry for an entire week.
gre.clue: staged noisy protests outside the ministry

example: Leaving dirty dishes in the hostel sink is the surest way to earn the ire of Mrs Akter, the strict warden.

en: Showing great attention to detail; very careful and precise
hook: METICULOUS: METIC-ulous, every metric measured perfectly.
story: Meticulous. Very careful and precise, attentive to every detail. Peter's mother stitches embroidered quilts in a quiet village. Each one takes months. She counts her stitches, unpicks any thread that wanders even slightly, and checks the pattern in daylight before every new row. When a buyer from the city examined one, she [gasp] could not find a single mistake. Her work is meticulous. The word comes from the Latin for fearful: a meticulous person is almost afraid of the smallest error. So, what word describes work done with great attention to every detail? ... Meticulous.

gre.s: The restoration took six years because the conservators were ____, cleaning the fresco one square centimeter at a time.
gre.clue: cleaning the fresco one square centimeter at a time

example: A meticulous tailor in Old Dhaka measured my father twelve times before cutting a single inch of cloth for his wedding suit.

en: Covered with a great deal of fancy decoration
hook: ORNATE: full of ORNAMENTS.
story: Ornate. Covered with a great deal of fancy decoration. Inside the old pink palace by the river, Dora stood still and stared. A grand staircase, crystal chandeliers, carved furniture and tall gilded mirrors filled every room. Even the ceilings seemed to curl with patterns. Her little sister [gasp] tugged her hand and pointed at everything at once. The palace was truly ornate. Ornate shares its root with ornament: an ornate room is full of ornaments. So, what word describes something richly covered in fancy decoration? ... Ornate.

gre.s: Critics accustomed to the novelist's spare, plain prose were surprised by the ____ style of his memoir, with its long, flowery sentences and extravagant metaphors.
gre.clue: with its long, flowery sentences and extravagant metaphors

example: The bride's ornate jamdani sari, woven with silver thread, took two weavers in Narayanganj almost four months to finish.

en: So intense or obvious that it can almost be touched or felt
hook: PALPABLE: you can PALPATE it, touch it with your hand.
story: Palpable. So intense or obvious that it can almost be touched. In the minutes before the final exam results came out, Nate's whole family sat around one phone. Nobody spoke. His mother held her tea without drinking it, and his father kept checking the time. The tension was palpable. Then the page loaded, and Nate [gasp] saw his name with top marks. His mother [sigh] finally drank her tea, and the relief was just as palpable. Palpable comes from the Latin for touch: palpable feelings are ones you can almost touch. So, what word describes tension so strong you can almost feel it? ... Palpable.

gre.s: As the verdict was read, the courtroom's tension was ____, and several spectators visibly held their breath.
gre.clue: several spectators visibly held their breath

example: Relief was palpable in the village when the floodwater finally began to drop after eleven days.

en: To make something, often bad, continue indefinitely
hook: PERPETUATE: make it PERPETUAL.
story: Perpetuate. To make something, often bad, continue for a long time. In Paul's office, new employees were always given the worst desks and the late shifts, simply because that was how the seniors had once been treated. Each year's juniors grew up and did the same to the next group. When Paul became a manager, he refused. "If we keep doing this, we perpetuate it forever." Perpetuate comes from perpetual, meaning lasting forever: to perpetuate a habit is to keep it going and going. So, what verb means to keep a bad practice alive? ... Perpetuate.

gre.s: Critics argue that the film's portrayal of the villagers as ignorant only serves to ____ stereotypes the director claimed to oppose.
gre.clue: stereotypes the director claimed to oppose

example: Paying ransom to the pirates, the admiral warned, would only perpetuate the kidnappings it was meant to stop.

en: A cunning plan or action designed to gain an advantage
hook: PLOY: a PLOT to deceive.
story: Ploy. A cunning plan or action designed to gain an advantage. Every evening at the old book market, one seller shouted, "Last copy! Last copy!" while waving a popular novel. Customers rushed to pay before it was gone. Arthur, a curious student, watched for an hour and noticed the seller pulling another last copy from a box under the table. Arthur [laugh] grinned. It was a clever ploy. Ploy sounds close to plot: a ploy is a small plot to win an advantage. So, what word names a cunning trick to get ahead? ... Ploy.

gre.s: Observers dismissed the minister's visit to the flooded villages, made days before the election with a dozen camera crews in tow, as a cynical ____ rather than a sincere act of compassion.
gre.clue: rather than a sincere act of compassion

example: The free trial was just a ploy to collect card numbers, and most users were charged the moment it ended.

en: Accurately predicting what will happen in the future
hook: PROPHETIC: like a PROPHET who foretells the future.
story: Prophetic. Accurately predicting what will happen. In the nineteen nineties, Shannon's grandfather, a coastal rice farmer, warned his neighbours that the salty tides were creeping farther inland each year. "One day our rice will not grow here," he said. People shook their heads and went home. Today, many of those fields have turned into shrimp ponds, and Shannon often remembers his words. They seem prophetic now. A prophet foretells the future, and prophetic words turn out to be true. So, what word describes a warning that later comes true? ... Prophetic.

gre.s: The economist's warnings, dismissed as alarmist when she first made them, proved ____ when the crisis struck exactly as she had predicted.
gre.clue: exactly as she had predicted

example: Written in 1949, the novel's picture of a society under constant surveillance now seems eerily prophetic.

en: To formally give up a claim, right, or belief
hook: RE-NOUNCE: an annouNCEment that you're giving it up.
story: Renounce. To formally give up a claim, right or belief. Neil's uncle owned a share of the family land, but he lived in Canada, and his sister farmed it alone to raise her children. One winter he flew home, sat with her before a lawyer, and signed a paper giving up his share forever. He renounced his claim so that her children would have security. Renounce shares a root with announce: you renounce something by announcing that you give it up. So, what verb means to formally give up a claim or right? ... Renounce.

gre.s: To accept the post, the businessman was required to ____ his foreign citizenship and divest himself of all private holdings.
gre.clue: divest himself of all private holdings

example: The heir shocked his family by renouncing his share of the tea estate and taking a small flat so he could work as a teacher.

en: Bravery shown when facing great danger, as in war
hook: VALOR: VALUE of a hero's courage.
story: Valor. Great bravery in the face of danger, as in war. Every December, Andy's grandfather takes out a faded photograph of young men in work shirts holding old rifles. In nineteen seventy-one, he was one of them, a freedom fighter crossing rivers at night during the war of independence. He rarely speaks of it, but the village honours him on Victory Day. Their valor is part of why their country exists. Valor shares a root with value, from the Latin for being strong: valor is strength of heart. So, what word means great bravery in battle? ... Valor.

gre.s: The soldier was decorated for his ____, having repeatedly crossed enemy lines under heavy fire to carry wounded comrades to safety.
gre.clue: having repeatedly crossed enemy lines under heavy fire

example: The firefighters who carried workers out of the burning factory were honoured for their valor at a ceremony in Dhaka.
